title: Agent nouns ending in -er
description: Nouns formed from a verb stem to name 'the person who does X' (an agent noun) almost always take der, e.g. lehren → der Lehrer. This is far more reliable than the bare -er ending in general, which is only masculine about 60% of the time overall.

exceptions.note: Ends in -er but is not an agent noun (window), so it falls outside this rule and is neuter instead.
A non-agentive -er word (mother) that is feminine, showing the rule only reliably applies to true agent/doer nouns.
Common -er noun (water) that is neuter, not an agent noun.

title: Nouns ending in -ling
description: Nouns ending in -ling, often naming a person or young creature characterized by a quality, are almost always masculine.

exceptions.note: A loanword (ship's railing) from Dutch/English that happens to end in -ling but is feminine — one of the few genuine exceptions.

title: Nouns ending in -ismus
description: Nouns borrowed from Greek/Latin with the ending -ismus, usually naming ideologies, movements, or conditions, are reliably masculine with essentially no exceptions.

title: Nouns ending in -or
description: Nouns ending in -or, many borrowed from Latin and often naming people, instruments, or abstract agents, are usually masculine.

exceptions.note: A native German word (gate/goal) that happens to end in -or but is neuter, not a Latin loanword.
Short for Laboratorium; neuter despite the -or ending.
Chemical element name (chlorine) — neuter, following the chemical-elements rule instead.

title: Nouns ending in -us
description: Nouns of Greek/Latin origin ending in -us are usually masculine.

exceptions.note: Grammatical term (gender) — neuter despite the -us ending.
A body of texts — neuter, a grammar/linguistics loanword exception.
Grammatical tense — neuter, part of a small cluster of neuter grammar terms in -us.

title: Nouns ending in -ant or -and
description: Nouns ending in -ant or -and, frequently naming a person who performs or undergoes an action (often from Latin participle forms), are usually masculine.

exceptions.note: French loanword ending in -ant that is neuter, not an agent noun.
Another French food loanword ending in -ant that is neuter rather than masculine.

title: Nouns ending in -eur/-ör
description: Nouns borrowed from French with the agent-noun ending -eur (sometimes -ör in older spellings) typically name a person and are masculine.

exceptions.note: Looks like it ends in -eur but is actually the unrelated native word Aben-teuer (adventure); neuter.
French loanword (color/character, used for fraternity colors) that is feminine rather than masculine.

title: Days, months, and seasons
description: Names of the days of the week, months of the year, and the four seasons are masculine.

exceptions.note: The year itself is neuter, even though it belongs to the calendar-units family.
The week is feminine, unlike the masculine day and month names.
Night is feminine, not masculine, despite belonging to the time-of-day family.
An alternative word for 'spring' that is neuter, contrasting with the standard masculine der Frühling.

title: Compass directions and precipitation
description: The four cardinal directions and most words for falling weather/precipitation are masculine. This covers precipitation specifically, not weather vocabulary in general, which is mixed.

exceptions.note: Sunshine is feminine, not masculine, despite being a common weather word.
Cloud is feminine, breaking the weather-is-masculine tendency.
Ice is neuter, not masculine.
Thunderstorm is neuter; the general word das Wetter (weather) itself is also neuter.

title: Alcoholic drinks
description: Most names of alcoholic drinks are masculine.

exceptions.note: Beer is the single most famous exception to the 'alcoholic drinks are masculine' rule; it is neuter.
A wine/fruit punch is feminine because it follows the common '-e ending is usually feminine' pattern instead.

title: Car brand names
description: When a manufacturer's name is used to mean 'a car of that make,' it takes der, following the gender of der Wagen (car).

exceptions.note: The same brand name takes die instead when it refers to a BMW motorcycle, following die Maschine/das Motorrad conventions rather than der Wagen.
The nickname for the Citroën 2CV ('duck') is feminine because it follows the everyday word Ente, not the car-brand rule.

title: Male persons and their roles
description: Nouns referring to male people or family roles are masculine, matching natural (biological) gender.

exceptions.note: 'Member' is neuter regardless of the person's sex — grammatical gender doesn't always track the referent's sex.
'Child' is neuter regardless of sex.
'Person' is grammatically feminine no matter who is being referred to, including men.

title: Nouns ending in -ung
description: Nouns formed from verbs with the ending -ung, usually describing an action or its result, are always feminine — one of the most reliable rules in German.

title: Nouns ending in -heit or -keit
description: Abstract nouns formed with -heit or -keit, usually from adjectives, are always feminine.

title: Nouns ending in -schaft
description: Nouns ending in -schaft, often naming collectives, states, or relationships, are always feminine.

title: Nouns ending in -tion or -sion
description: Nouns borrowed from Latin/French with the endings -tion or -sion, common in formal and academic vocabulary, are always feminine.

title: Nouns ending in -tät
description: Nouns ending in -tät, borrowed from Latin abstract nouns in -tas, are always feminine.

title: Nouns ending in -ie
description: Nouns ending in -ie, many borrowed from Greek/Latin abstract or scientific vocabulary, are usually feminine.

exceptions.note: 'Genius' is neuter despite the -ie ending.
An English loanword referring to a person; masculine rather than feminine because it names a person type.

title: Nouns ending in -ik
description: Nouns ending in -ik, especially names of academic fields and disciplines, are usually feminine.

exceptions.note: Refers to a male Catholic person, so it is masculine rather than following the -ik-is-feminine pattern.

title: Nouns ending in -in for female people/animals
description: Adding -in to a masculine noun for a person or animal creates the feminine counterpart, which is always feminine.

exceptions.note: 'Appointment' ends in -in but is an unrelated masculine word, not a feminine-agent form.
French loanword ending in -in that is neuter, unrelated to the feminizing suffix.
'Ruby' ends in -in but is masculine — the ending here is coincidental, not the feminizing suffix.

title: Nouns ending in -ur
description: Nouns ending in -ur, many borrowed from Latin/French abstract and technical vocabulary, are usually feminine.

exceptions.note: The school-leaving exam is neuter despite the -ur ending.
'Purple/crimson' is masculine, not feminine.
'Hallway/corridor' is masculine, a common everyday exception to the -ur pattern.

title: Nouns ending in -enz or -anz
description: Abstract nouns borrowed from Latin with the endings -enz or -anz are always feminine.

title: Nouns ending in -e
description: Many native German nouns ending in -e are feminine — roughly 90% of them — making it a useful but imperfect first guess rather than a firm rule.

exceptions.note: 'Cheese' ends in -e but is masculine.
'Eye' ends in -e but is neuter.
'End' ends in -e but is neuter.
'Boy' ends in -e but is masculine, matching natural gender rather than the suffix pattern.
'Interest' ends in -e but is neuter.

title: Trees, flowers, and fruits
description: Most native names of trees, flowers, and fruits are feminine.

exceptions.note: Apple is masculine — it ends in -el, which pulls it into the masculine -el pattern instead.
Maple is one of the best-known masculine tree exceptions.
Dandelion is masculine, not feminine.
Poppy is masculine.
Lilac is masculine, ending in -er like many masculine nouns.

title: German, Austrian, and Swiss rivers
description: Most rivers within German-speaking countries are feminine. This is only a strong tendency, not an absolute rule — river gender is largely historical and often has to be memorized individually.

exceptions.note: The Rhine, one of the most important German rivers, is masculine, not feminine.
The Main river is masculine.
The Neckar river is masculine.

title: Female persons and their roles
description: Nouns referring to female people or family roles are feminine, matching natural (biological) gender.

exceptions.note: 'Girl' is neuter, not feminine, because the diminutive suffix -chen always overrides natural gender and forces neuter.
The old-fashioned word for 'young lady/miss' is neuter for the same reason: the -lein diminutive suffix forces neuter.
An old/blunt word for 'woman' that is neuter rather than feminine, an irregular historical holdover.

title: Diminutives ending in -chen or -lein
description: Adding the diminutive suffix -chen or -lein to any noun always makes it neuter, regardless of the original noun's gender. This override is essentially exceptionless.

title: Nouns ending in -um
description: Nouns borrowed from Latin with the ending -um are usually neuter.

exceptions.note: 'Consumption' is masculine despite the -um ending.
'Rum' happens to end in the letters -um but is masculine, not an instance of the Latin -um suffix.

title: Nouns ending in -ment
description: Nouns borrowed from Latin/French with the ending -ment are usually neuter.

exceptions.note: Meaning 'a point in time,' this common word is masculine (das Moment exists separately with the more technical meaning 'factor/momentum').
'Cement' is masculine, not neuter.

title: Nouns ending in -tum
description: Abstract nouns ending in -tum, often naming states, systems, or collectives, are usually neuter. This is a strong tendency rather than an absolute rule, since two very common -tum words are masculine.

exceptions.note: 'Wealth' is masculine, one of the two best-known exceptions to the -tum-is-neuter pattern.
'Error/mistake' is masculine, the other well-known exception.

title: Collective nouns with the Ge- prefix
description: Nouns formed with the collective prefix Ge- (often also ending in -e), naming a group or repeated activity, are usually neuter. There are around twenty common exceptions.

exceptions.note: 'Thought' is masculine, not neuter, despite the Ge- prefix.
'Taste' is masculine, an exception to the Ge-is-neuter pattern.
'Story/history' is feminine, not neuter.
'Danger' is feminine despite starting with Ge-.

title: Nominalized (verb) infinitives
description: Any verb's bare infinitive can be turned into a noun (capitalized, used like the English '-ing' form: essen → das Essen), and the result is always neuter, with no exceptions.

title: Nouns ending in -icht
description: A cluster of common native German nouns ending in -icht are neuter.

exceptions.note: 'View/sight' ends in -icht but is feminine.
'Duty' ends in -icht but is feminine.

title: Nouns ending in -o
description: Nouns ending in -o, mostly modern loanwords, are usually neuter.

exceptions.note: The currency name is masculine despite ending in -o.
The Italian coffee loanword is masculine.
This Spanish food loanword ending in -o is feminine, not neuter.

title: Nouns ending in -ma
description: Nouns of Greek origin ending in -ma are usually neuter.

exceptions.note: 'Company/firm' ends in -ma but is feminine, one of the best-known exceptions.
This loanword ends in -ma but is masculine, not neuter.

title: Nouns ending in -nis or -sal
description: Roughly two-thirds of nouns ending in -nis (and most ending in -sal) are neuter, but a substantial minority of -nis words are feminine instead — this is a lean, not a reliable rule, so each word should be checked individually.

exceptions.note: 'Knowledge' ends in -nis but is feminine, part of the large feminine minority in this group.
'Permission' ends in -nis but is feminine.
'Realization/insight' ends in -nis but is feminine.
'Wilderness' ends in -nis but is feminine.

title: Metals and chemical elements
description: Names of metals and chemical elements are usually neuter.

exceptions.note: Steel (technically an alloy, not a pure element) is masculine.
Bronze (an alloy) is feminine, following the -e ending pattern instead.
Sulfur is masculine, ending in -el like many masculine nouns.
Phosphorus is masculine, following the -or ending pattern instead of the metals/elements pattern.

title: Colors used as nouns
description: When a color adjective is used as a noun (e.g. 'the blue of the sky'), it is always neuter.

title: Countries, continents, and cities
description: Most country, continent, and city names are grammatically neuter and normally used without any article at all (e.g. simply 'Deutschland,' not 'das Deutschland'). A closed list of countries takes a different, obligatory article instead.

exceptions.note: Switzerland is feminine and always used with the article, unlike most countries.
Turkey is feminine and always takes an article, like other countries ending in -ei.
Iran is masculine and always takes an article.
Iraq is masculine and always takes an article.
Used only in the plural (die Vereinigten Staaten), unlike the singular neuter default for most countries.

title: Young people and baby animals
description: Many nouns for young/immature humans and animals are neuter, even when the adult form has a different gender.

exceptions.note: 'Puppy' is masculine, not neuter, despite naming a baby animal.
'Larva/grub' (an immature insect) is feminine, not neuter.

title: Letters of the alphabet
description: Individual letters of the alphabet, used as nouns, are neuter.

exceptions.note: The generic word for 'letter' (as in 'a letter of the alphabet') is itself masculine, not neuter.
